Canadian Camping 





EDITORIAL 


m 

SPIRITUAL 
ASPECTS 
OF CAMPMO 


Once upon a time by the restless 
shores of the Pacific, I had a camp for 
’teen-aged boys . . . one hundred of 
them . . . happy and carefree, strong, 
athletic and filled with the spirit of 
adventure. The camp was astir with 
excitement and activity, for on the 
morrow, nineteen carefully chosen boys 
were to climb the Western Lion which 
towered for over a mile high, with 
precipitous crags, directly above the 
camp. 

Well shod and with pack sacks 
filled to the full, we slowly and labouri- 
ously followed the trail, pausing at 
times to rest or to assist a struggling 
climber. At last, the “Back” was reach¬ 
ed; we parked our packs and attacked 
the “Head”. Here were real hazards 
and perilous slopes. However, the peak 
was reached and the descent began, 
and we safely reached the plateau. 

The packs were opened, a fire was 
kindled, and we had our evening meal. 
Then, far to the West, a glorious golden 
sunset was so silently unveiled! It was 
breath taking! 

One boy said, “Let’s sing something!” 

Then one boy, a lad from whom I 
least expected it, said, “Let’s sing, ‘Unto 
the hills around do I lift up my longing 
eyes’ 


By The Right Rev. A. H. Sovereign , 
M.A., D.D ., F.R.G.S. 


On the mountain top, facing the 
flaming sunset, the hardy, stalwart boys 
worshipped The Eternal . . . and then, 
to sleep. 

“Yon glorious sky His temple stands, 

So lofty, bright and blue, 

All lamped with stars and curtained 
round 

With clouds of every hue.” 

Boys not religious? Oh, they are 
deeply religious, if you know the boy 
and if you understand religion. 

What is the purpose of a camp? 
What are we trying to do? It is the 
aim which moulds the camp, its pro¬ 
gramme and the campers. It is analo¬ 
gous to education, and the definitions 
coincide. “Education is the training in 
right living”, “the unfolding of the 
innate powers of personality”, “not 
learning to make a living but learning 
to live”, “the development of the full¬ 
ness of life”. 

What is personality? It is the unity 
of the impulses, drives and interests of 
the individual at any one time. No 
better definition has ever been given 
than that of Dr. Luke, the Greek 
physician: “Jesus increased in wisdom 
and stature, and in favour of God and 
man.” Personality is that which lifts 


Toronto , Canada , April 1958 


109 




man above the animal world, and links 
him with the Divine. 

We, therefore, think of the person 
under the four aspects of the physical, 
the intellectual, the spiritual and the 
social. But this personal quadrilateral 
is a unity; it cannot be divided. The 
Faculty Psychology of fifty years ago 
is as dead as a dodo. 

After an address by a boy leader, a 
member of the audience asked, “And 
what about religion?” The answer was, 
“We teach the boy to tie knots and to 
build bridges, but we leave it to the 
parson to teach him religion.” But you 
cannot work by that policy; the boy is 
not built on the compartment plan; 
he is ONE. 

What is religion? What is worship? 
It has its origin in the word “worth” 
. . . “worthship”. It is reverence which 
is given to that which is worthy, 
whether in God or man. In the evolu¬ 
tion of ideas and words, an interesting 
family has come to us, and all descend 
from the same root, “weal” . . . wealth 
(well-being), whole, wholesome, hale, 
halig (holy), health. In other words, 
the “whole” life is “holy”. Religion (the 
spiritual) is not something superim¬ 
posed on personality; it is part and 
parcel of the whole life which naturally 
becomes wholesome. Religion is not 
something to be “put into youth”; it 
is an innate faculty or power to be 
drawn from him; it is already within 
him, awaiting the magic touch of a 
master to reveal it. 

Education comes from “e-duco” — 
to lead out from. The spiritual is not 
something to be associated only with a 
Church Service or our Outdoor Chapel. 
It should permeate every part of life, 
everywhere, always. In a camp, the 
spiritual is the natural atmosphere of 
the games, the hikes, the meals, the 
songs, the talks, the vesper hour. No 
one names it; no one apologizes for it. 

God, the Eternal, the Infinite, is not 
far away in some distant heaven, but 
is ever-present everywhere . . . “closer 


than hands and feet, closer than breath 
itself”. The first and deepest words for 
God are “spirit”, “breath”, Ruach 
(Hebrew), Pneuma (Greek) and Spiri- 
tus (Latin). 

“Breathe on me, Breath of God”. 
God is not only present in a Temple 
made with hands, but in the Temple 
of the Eternal Hills. “The Heavens are 
telling the Glory of God”. 

I hesitate to speak of youth “finding 
God”, as if God hides Himself from 
man; but rather that youth has “an 
awareness of God”. God really is seek¬ 
ing man as portrayed so dramatically 
in “The Hound of Heaven” by Francis 
Thompson. 

In a camp with the proper atmos¬ 
phere, each camper by unconscious nu¬ 
trition lives in “the awareness of God”. 
God, the Eternal is Holiness, Truth, 
Beauty, Love, Goodness, and completely 
in the Hero of Youth, Jesus of Naza¬ 
reth, the King of Youth. If you wish 
to send a message, wrap it up in a 
person. That is just what The Eternal 
did! 

Naturally, the spiritual aspects of a 
camp must be wrapped up in the Camp 
Director. He (or she) unconsciously 
but effectively must radiate this divine 
spark. He must create this “awareness 
of God”. It was said of a certain Direc¬ 
tor of a girls’ camp, “her face shone 
with a spiritual glow”. Then, this ra¬ 
diating atmosphere is infused into the 
minds and hearts of carefully chosen 
and well-trained counsellors, and then 
to each and every camper. It is like the 
measles, it is caught, not taught. This 
spirit of “the Good and the Beautiful” 
is instilled into the whole of the camp 
life so that nothing that is ugly or 
obscene can find a place. There is an 
expulsive power in the presence of the 
Highest. 

The camp site, separated from high¬ 
ways and life’s “fierce confusion” looks 
far into the Western stillness, over lake 
and hills to the sky and God’s glorious 

continued on page 139 


MO 


Canadian Camping 


Marilyn Ward was the Plays and 
Music Counsellor at the Junior League 
Camp for girls, during the 1957 season. 
The Camp is subsidized by the Junior 
League of Montreal and accommodates 
over one hundred girls for three weeks, 
three times during the summer. 

Play-making is one of the four sched¬ 
uled activities. Participation in each 
activity, except swimming, is voluntary. 
In the eight years that this kind of 
theater has been part of the regular 
daily routine, there has been no lack of 
participation. It seems to appeal to all 
age groups, although enthusiasm may 
vary between the Juniors, the Inter¬ 
mediates and the Seniors, each term. 
We stay pretty much on the level of 
plays made from stories. A few young¬ 
sters who want to improve their skills 
(as in any activity) may want to add 
the business of learning to memorize 
lines from scripts, but there is hardly 
time for this in a- short term camp. We 
avoid play-writing since girls of 8-16 
have not the knowledge or the tech¬ 
nique necessary to produce an ‘actable’ 
play. With thousands of stories to 
choose from it seems best to avoid the 
possibility that the play-writes will tell 
more of their personal affairs than they 
intend. 

Sunday Evening is Theater Night. 
The first Sunday, a few days after they 
arrive, we have Talent Night. This is 
built around a theme with the object 
of getting participants to perform in 
groups and avoid embarrassing the 
individual who is more hopeful than 
skillful. 

Plays are performed on-stage or as 
Theater-in-the-round, inside. Competi¬ 
tion from mosquitoes, wind and rain is 
too great for amateurs. However, it is 
not a ‘foul weather’ programme since 
the practices can be held outside on 
the camp-site or on hikes. 

The fact that the audiences are com- 


PLAY 

MAKING 

A New Approach to Programme 
By MARILYN WARD 

with a Foreword by 

Agnes Mutchlcr , Director 
Junior League Camp, Montreal, Quo. 


posed of actors, makes for closer atten¬ 
tion to what goes on on-stage. Most of 
the children will have had at least a 
walk-on part before they leave and 
enjoyed being someone else—within a 
prescribed pattern for a few minutes. 
Besides it is great fun to have Sunday 
suppers with giants, bunnies, dashing 
knights and beautifully dressed ladies! 
Although this article deals exclusively 
with Play-making at a Girl’s camp, the 
same activity, carefully set up, can 
interest boys or both boys and girls as 
well. Youngsters are always acting! 

Marilyn Ward had the two qualities 
necessary to develop this activity; a 
wealth of reading and an understanding 
of people. Some knowledge of theater 
techniques is helpful, but the important 
thing is to play it straight, get fun out 
of the situations and make the story 
clear to the audience. 

—Agnes Mutchler 

Playmaking, more than any other 
form of dramatics, provides an oppor¬ 
tunity for creative self-expression, a 


Toronto , Canada , April 1958 


111 



necessity for children of all ages. It 
helps, if handled carefully, in the devel¬ 
opment of their behaviour also, as the 
energy of the over-aggresive child can 
by this means be channelled along lines 
more desirable than those which she 
might choose for herself, and the shy 
or withdrawn child can gain confidence 
from this kind of activity ,and a feeling 
of importance in the group, for whether 
her role be large or small, it contributes 
to the success of the play just as much 
as the others. The practicing of the 
plays must, of course, be done in groups, 
and it is in this respect that Plays con¬ 
tributes a great deal to the overall pro¬ 
gramme of the camp, as work and play 
in groups is one of the fundamental 
principles of camping. But aside from 
the psychological and sociological as¬ 
pects of this kind of activity, Plays are 
simply good fun; fun to act, and fun to 
direct, and the Sunday night entertain¬ 
ment offers a change in the regular 
evening programme which is, I trust, a 
pleasant one for campers and counsel¬ 
lors alike. 

Every week, four to six stories are 
chosen by the Head of Plays in collab¬ 
oration with the counsellors assigned to 
Plays for that week. Each story is told 
(not read) to a group of children, who 
then discuss with their Counsellor the 
best way of dramatizing it. (It takes 
considerable time and patience to con¬ 
vince some of the counsellors that this 
is a better method than that of reading 
the story and memorizing the dialogue, 
but experiences this summer have shown 
that it is by far the more successful). 
Most of the programme time throughout 
the rest of the week is spent practising 
the play, which grows and develops as 
it goes along, using in some way or 
another all those who present themselves 
for Plays. It is best not to cast the play 
too early in the week, as each child 
should have the opportunity to play 
several roles before choosing a definite 


one, and this also makes it easier to 
substitute in the event that any of them 
should be unable or unwilling to per¬ 
form on the Sunday night. Incidentally, 
this year, there was only one occasion 
on which an unwillingness to perform 
was shown, and I think that speaks well 
for the atmosphere created in Plays by 
the counsellors concerned. 

Each counsellor makes a 1 folder, in 
which she outlines the main action in 
each scene of her play, keeps a list of 
characters and of the children in her 
group, and makes notes concerning 
scenery, lighting, props, etc. This helps 
her to keep clearly in mind a T l aspects 
of her play, and also enables the Head 
of Plays or another counsellor to take 
over without much difficulty on her 
day off. Costumes for the play should 
be selected as early as possible during 
the week, and scenery also should be 
well under way by Wednesday. 

For the scenery used in our plays a 
set of screens, two double, one triple, 
and one quadruple, are used. These 
screens may be folded in many ways, 
and may be arranged in numerous com¬ 
binations, the most effective being those 
which provide for two sets of scenery 
on the stage at the same time, one on 
each side. This allows for the plays to 
run smoothly, especially since the lights 
on each side of the stage work inde¬ 
pendently and a change of scene means 
merely the switching off of the light on 
one side of the stage, and the switching 
on of the other. Moreover, the interval 
between the plays (during which the 
audience sings songs), is shortened 
because the back of the screens may be 
used for the scenery of other plays, and 
so all that is required is the reversal 
of the screens. To further facilitate the 
mounting of scenery, large paper clips, 
such as those used on slip boards, are 
used in lieu of thumb tacks, as one such 
clip can hold two pieces of scenery to 
one screen, one on the back and one on 


112 


Canadian Camping 



the front, and can be clipped on or off 
very quickly. 

On Sunday afternoon at 4 o’clock, 
the casts of all the plays arrive at Chat- 
aqua for their costumes and make-up. 
The costumes have by then been sel¬ 
ected and placed on hangers on the left 
hand side of the stage in labelled play 
groups, and each Plays counsellor this 
year was made responsible for her own 
group of costumes. She helps the cam¬ 
pers to change and hang their clothes 
on the right hand side of the stage, 
after which they join one of the make¬ 
up lines. This summer, (especially dur¬ 
ing the first term) several counsellors 
other than those directing their own 
plays, offered their assistance, and their 
help was invaluable. While two or 
three counsellors were mounting scenery 
on the stage, the rest were seated on the 
edge of the stage, each with a supply 
of make-up and a line of campers wait¬ 
ing to be transformed into some char¬ 
acter of long ago or from far away. As 
soon as each child had been made up, 
she was sent back to her circle in readi¬ 
ness for supper, as the counsellors were 
too busy to cope with a large group of 
excited campers all of whom were in 
high spirits by this time. The reason for 
dressing before supper is not only that 
there is more time then, but also that 
Sunday is visitors’ day, and those cam¬ 
pers who might be feeling a little home¬ 
sick after seeing their parents — and 
those, too, who are feeling lonely be¬ 
cause their parents did not arrive at all 
— have something exciting to capture 
their attention and cheer them up as 
soon as the visitors leave in the after¬ 
noon. 

Supper, then, is eaten in costume, 
and directly afterwards the players 
leave the table and go to Ghataqua, 
where finishing touches are put to 
lipstick and hair, wings are pinned on 
again, crowns are put straight, and 
other such important items are seen to. 


When all is ready, the players are 
seated in rows on the floor with their 
counsellors, those in the first play being 
in the front row, and so on. Usually 
we have a sing-song until the other 
campers arrive, as this helps to some 
extent to calm down those whose 
nervousness and excitement would 
otherwise be demonstrated by means of 
unruly or noisy behaviour.

(Jun. and Int.)

AMONG 

OURSELVES 


By Adele Stalten Ebbs , Director, 
Camp Wapomeo 


The last fifty years have seen the 
birth of organized camping; its infancy, 
adolescence and adulthood. Wallace 
Forgie has participated in all stages of 
this development as camper, leader, 
director and honorary director. His 
camping experiences have been unique 
because he has dared to pioneer un¬ 
known fields; his achievements have 
been great because he has courageously 
surmounted obstacles, and tenaciously 
clung to his goals. 

Mr. Forgie was born in Ottawa but 
soon moved with his family to Toronto. 
This was not the last that Ottawa was 
going to know of her native son. In 
Toronto he came under the influence 
of the leaders in the Y.M.C.A. In ’99 
he joined the Leaders’ Corps and with 
Mr. Howard Crocker as director, went 
to his first camp at Lake Scugog. In 
1905, when Camp Couchiching “Y” 
camp opened, he was a tent leader. 
Here Mr. Forgie had his first associa¬ 
tion with Taylor Statten, a friendship 
and working partnership which con¬ 
tinued through the years. 

The next thirty years of Mr. Forgie’s 
life were devoted to the Y.M.C.A. 
Whenever there was a demanding job 
to be done, the services of this vigorous 
man were sought. By his leadership he 



Wallace Forgie 


could change a destructive “gang” into 
a well-organized, purposeful group of 
young people, winning their loyalty 
through stimulating recreational and 
athletic programmes. In Ottawa, he 
built the foundations for On-da-da- 
waks camp, which has become one of 
the most vital Y.M.C.A. camps in the 
country. From now on, camping was 
to be Mr. Forgie’s chief interest in 
whatever job he was doing. 

The two world wars were interrup¬ 
tions in this chosen pattern of life. He 
was Toronto Boys’ Work Secretary 
when he volunteered for service the 
day war was declared in 1914. His five 
year period overseas again pioneered 
new areas. Because of his driving per¬ 
sonality, the Y.M.C.A. became a vital 
factor in the life of our troops. During 
the second world war, he was available 
for any trouble spot in Canada where 
the troops needed assistance in recrea¬ 
tion or in personnel problems. 


114 


Canadian Camping 



In 1920, Mr. Forgie went to Calgary 
as secretary of the newly formed Boys’ 
Work Board. Camping was, as usual, 
the core of his programme. It is inter¬ 
esting to camp people that Dr. Hedley 
S. Dimock had the comparable job in 
Saskatchewan at this time, and that it 
was Professor Charles E. Hendry who 
took over the job in Alberta when Mr. 
Forgie moved on to India in 1927. For 
nine years Mr. Forgie worked for the 
Y.M.C.A. in South India and Ceylon. 
He did a survey and set up an educa¬ 
tional programme which, naturally, for 
him included camping. His camping 
experiences were varied and numerous, 
handicapped by poor sites, lack of 
equipment and little understanding of 
his objectives by those with whom he 
worked. 

All this time he had in his mind the 
idea of setting up a demonstration area 
which was eventually realized in the 
establishment of Camp Tonakela, near 
Madras. It was his dream come true, 
made possible by the loyal support and 
practical assistance of friends in this 
country who believed in him and in his 
enterprise. The bond of mutual support 
and interest was firmly established in 
1938 when Mr. and Mrs. Taylor Statten 
went to Madras to officially open the 
camp and extend greetings from the 
Canadian Camping Association. Quot¬ 
ing from “The Madras Mail” January 
17, 1938, “The camp, site and equip¬ 
ment is the gift of an overseas fellow¬ 
ship of girl and boy campers in Canada 
and the United States.” All that has 
come before seems to be the forerunner 
of what will stand out as Mr. Forgie’s 
greatest contribution to the world. 

The need for this camp was so 
clearly proven to forward looking, 
youth-minded people over there, that 
operation, temporarily interrupted dur¬ 
ing the war, was soon re-established. 
On February twenty-first of this year, 
Tonakela celebrated its twenty-first 


birthday. Its influence and usefulness 
has broadened into new fields of ser¬ 
vice to include last year: camping for 
2,764 children and young adults in 
thirty-seven camp groups, serving in 
various ways according to their needs; 
schools, scouts and guides, blind, 
orphans and certified children; con¬ 
valescent care for 101; minor medical 
treatment for 3,910; and special feed¬ 
ing once-a-day, serving 12,133 meals. 
From the director’s report, “In the 
Camp Log they write their hearty 
thanks to the Committee here and to 
the people overseas who made camp 
available to them.” 

Some fortunate Canadians and 
friends from the United States have 
visited Camp Tonakela. Their reports 
are most enthusiastic. In every case 
they have been impressed by the high 
place Mr. Forgie holds in the regard 
of his friends in the countryside sur¬ 
rounding the camp. As he walks 
through the neighbouring villages from 
which children come to Tonakela for a 
daily meal, the families emerge from 
their huts and greet him with affection 
and devotion. For those who have not 
had the opportunity to visit, it was an 
inspiration to spend time with N. Peru- 
mal Naidu who travelled widely in 
Canada and the United States with 
Mr. Forgie in 1956. The devotion of 
that one Indian was a clue to the 
feel mgs his other countrymen must 
have. Since then, Perumal has become 
camp d : r.3ctor and Mr. Forgie has 
happily handed over this great responsi- 
b : Jity to one whom he has trained and 
in whom he has complete confidence. 

Tonakela, in Ojibway, as well as in 
a South Indian dialect, means “you 
first” and it is truly well named. Wallace 
Forgie has dedicated his life to this 
great idea which is now firmly estab¬ 
lished and will continue with our 
support as a factor towards better 
understanding and world peace. 


Toronto, Canada , April 1958 


115 



FROM THE 
PRESIDENT’S DESK 


By F. M. Van Wagner, 
Director, Camp Nominingue. 


Canada is, without question, a won¬ 
derful camping country. From coast to 
coast are vast lake-studded forest areas 
and majestic mountain ranges beckon¬ 
ing all to leave the crowded highways 
for quieter trails, where nature at its 
best may be enjoyed. For most Can¬ 
adians, ideal camping country is close 
at hand. Such being our heritage, it 
might be supposed that in large num¬ 
bers our people would, in all seasons, 
seek their recreation in the out-of-doors. 
Unfortunately, this does not seem to be 
the case. 

We know of no more enjoyable and 
worthwhile form of recreation than 
camping, and such related activities as 
hiking, canoeing, skiing, photography 
and the enjoyment of nature in all its 
forms. But as we are not campers by 
nature, these interests must be acquired, 
preferably during our younger days. 
Most boys and girls readily develop an 
interest in camping if introduced to it 
by skilful leaders. Nowhere are condi¬ 
tions so favourable for such training as 
in our summer camps, and it seems 
logical that camps should place major 
emphasis on developing an interest in 
all that pertains to the enjoyment of 
life in the open. A real camping ex¬ 
perience would then be a natural out¬ 
come of a season at camp. 

Though camp directors frequently ex¬ 
press a desire to attach more impor¬ 
tance to what is referred to as “real 
camping,” there is, I am, afraid, often 
quite a gap between the good intentions 
and what is actually accomplished. 


If our camps today are failing in this 
all-important duty, the responsibility for 
the situation rests with us directors. 

This situation may in part result 
from the fact that, while camp directors 
may be good administrators, they are 
not always experienced and skilful 
campers. The director who has never 
been on a camping trip, or who has 
no desire for close personal contact 
with the woods, a tent, pack or paddle, 
is hardly the best person to promote 
camping activities among his campers. 

There is no reason why, in such case, 
he should not secure for his staff a 
mature, experienced person, well versed 
in skills associated with camping, and 
with the ability to organize such ac¬ 
tivities for campers. 

We realize that the camp programme 
must provide for a wide variety of 
interests. We would not suggest that 
camping activities should be promoted 
to the exclusion of all else. There ac¬ 
tually seems little danger that this will 
happen. The real danger is that we wdl 
more and more turn to the programmes 
with which we are most familiar and 
are easiest to promote, while failing to 
introduce our campers to the things 
that will give a lasting appreciation of 
what we have referred to as our na¬ 
tural heritage. 

This seems a good time for each of 
us to review past practice to see if a 
way can be found to give our boys and 
girls a fuller camping experience in the 
season ahead. 


116 


Canadian Camping 





By Elizabeth Wardley Raymer. 
Director } Camp Tanamakoon 


HOW CAN 
WE HELP? 



Last summer in a spirit of nostalgia, 
I returned to a campsite I had known 
and loved as a canoe-tripping coun¬ 
sellor in the thirties. From the lake, it 
was still a place of beauty. The perfect 
sandy landing spot was as I remem¬ 
bered it. I climbed the little path to the 
camping ground and was appalled! The 
neat fireplace of memory was a hodge 
podge of scattered rocks. It contained 
a nauseating mass of half-rotten gar¬ 
bage which would have to be cleaned 
up before a fire could be built. I sat 
down on a frowsy hatchet-scarred log. 
Immediately a cloud of house flies ap¬ 
peared and sat on me. Driven to activity 
to shake this filthy welcoming commit¬ 
tee, I toured the entire site. There were 
three mountains of rustifig tin cans 
within fifty feet of the fireplace. It 
would take a Paul Bunyan to flatten, 
bum and bury these! Eyes and nose 
told me that no latrine had been dug 
here’ for a long, long time. Knife and 
axe-marred remains of a table and 
shelter showed where campers had 
gathered fuel for their fires. Those 
jewel-like gleams reflecting the sunlight 
from the ground came from broken 
glass. Bits of food and vegetable scrap¬ 
ings undulated in the shallow water, 
an invitation to leeches. There was no 
clean place to put down a sleeping bag 
or a blanket. I felt a pagan impulse to 
prostrate myself in apology to nature 
for intruding on this spot of shame. 

Angry questions raced through my 
mind. What about the sacred obligation 
to leave every campsite in better condi¬ 


tion than one found it? What about 
burning every scrap of unsavoury evi¬ 
dence that this place had been occu¬ 
pied? What about leaving a clean, tidy, 
fire-safely-extinguished fireplace, and a 
pile of wood for the next comer? How 
could such a slum come to be? Who 
had done this dreadful thing? 

As a private citizen I could quite 
honestly absolve myself from blame. But 
as a camp director my conscience can¬ 
not rest. What are we teaching these 
children under our care? How are we 
“moulding” these citizens of tomorrow? 
Do they regard the wonders of the 
forest and the beauties of the outdoors 
as a hallowed trust, a precious loan to 
them? Is a hike, a cookout, or a canoe 
trip a worthwhile excursion into pio¬ 
neering days or a slum inspection tour? 
Are campers learning to accept passive¬ 
ly and put up with such conditions? 
Are they contributing to them with a 
We-Know-Better-but-What’s-the-Use 
attitude ? 

How effective is our supervision? 
When campers leave camp does it carry 
over in such a way that they are filled 
with a zeal to be worthy trippers who 
are truly at home in and in sympathy 
with the outdoors? Or, are our campers 
under such restraint that they literally 
blow their tops when they are out of 
sight? 

We have all observed the peculiar 
behaviour of pent-up adults who feel

DEAR PARENTS . 

A Gamp Director’s' Letter to parents on the By Ed H. Devitt, 

methods and values of camping. Director , Camp Comak 


Camping has been described as “a 
creative, educational experience in co¬ 
operative group living in the out-of- 
doors.” Some parents make the mistake 
of thinking that the camp assumes most, 
if not all, responsibility for making this 
experience a valuable one. Actually the 
experience is most valuable only when it 
is a completely cooperative undertaking 
involving campers and parents and the 
camp. The camper must participate 
with interest and enthusiasm, the camp 
must supply essential leadership^ and 
facilities, parents must supply continuing 
guidance and leadership, and all must 
understand and appreciate camping’s 
far-reaching possibilities, its basic aims, 
principles and methods. 

Our first premise, of course, is that 
camp is “camper-centred”, that it exists 
primarily for the benefit of the camper. 
Its basic aim, then, can be said to help 
the camper enjoy a happy, carefree, 
worthwhile and purposeful experience 
in the out-of-doors. Through this ex¬ 
perience, we expect that the camper 
will have the opportunity to express 
his or her personality and develop in 
character through creative, stimulating 
activity, associations and work to de¬ 
velop outdoor skills; to practise the art 
of group living; to develop an under¬ 
standing and appreciation of the out- 
of-doors, and significant social, moral 
and spiritual values. This represents a 
tremendous challenge and explains why 
camping is considered to be the most 
important development in modern edu¬ 
cational and recreational fields. 


Because camp has the advantage of 
being, to a large extent, a controlled 
environment in which the director and 
staff bring together the facilities, leader¬ 
ship and influences desired, we have 
reason, to believe that many of these 
hoped-for results can be achieved. On 
the other hand, camp has one serious 
limitation: time. The camp environ¬ 
ment exists for only a few weeks each 
year; the basic, fundamental environ¬ 
ment of home, school, church and com¬ 
munity carries on for at least ten 
months of every year. The camper is 
mainly the product of this home envir¬ 
onment. Camp can supplement this 
environment by helping to expand inter¬ 
ests and activities, by shaping behaviour 
patterns and by enlarging appreciation 
of true values. As a result, we have 
reason to expect that camp will con¬ 
tribute much, but we should not expect 
it to contribute beyond its capabilities. 
With campers, parents and the camp 
working together in * full-and free co¬ 
operation, in spite of our limitations, 
together we should be able to achieve 
valuable .results. 

What can the camp do to help 
accomplish these results? First and 
foremost, it can do all in its power to 
make camp a safe and happy place 
for your child. Health and ; safety do 
not just happen at camp, as some people 
used to assume. They are secured and 
maintained only through sustained effort 
and eternal vigilance. The director is 
aware that through lack of proper care 
and supervision camp could even be an 


118 


Canadian Camping 



unsafe and unhealthy place. Therefore 
fundamental requirements must be met. 
Campers themselves must be safety and 
health-conscious, understanding, the 
factors involved and the procedures 
followed. They must agree that it is 
better to be safe than sorry, to err in 
the direction of overcautiousness with¬ 
out losing the sense of adventure. 
Campers and counsellors should remem¬ 
ber, at a point of decision, the saying, 
“If in doubt, don’t do it”. 

Camps follow provincial Health De¬ 
partment regulations regarding water 
and milk supply, food preparation and 
storage, dish-washing, and garbage dis¬ 
posal methods, fly and insect control, 
living quarters etc. They follow Camp¬ 
ing Association standards regarding gen¬ 
eral health and sanitation, water-front 
safety and leadership. Health standards 
require a graduate camp nurse on staff 
and a doctor in camp or on call. Camps 
provide planned, balanced, substantial 
meals, keeping in mind the requirements 
of all campers and also individual cam¬ 
pers. Your child may lose weight slightly 
during the first ten days due to strenu¬ 
ous camp living, but should then regain 
normal weight and add to it. Special 
provision can be made for individual 
campers to try to gain or lose weight 
through special diets. 

Camp takes into account the rest and 
sleep requirements of your child, always 
allowing for individual differences. 
There is a rest period of at least one 
hour after the noon meal, and this can 
be extended for campers who require 
it. The camp is also aware of the* 
possibility of over-stimulation through 
active group living, and takes steps to 
avoid it. A camp period should start 
and end on a leisurely note, and pro¬ 
ceed at the proper pace for the varying 
physical capabilities and emotional 
characteristics of the campers. Some 
thrive on great activity, others require 


periods of rest and relaxation. The 
over-all program, therefore, should 
reach the “golden mean” between too 
much activity and not enough. Cam¬ 
pers should go about their activities 
happily and purposefully with some¬ 
thing worth while to do when they 
want to do it, but without a feeling of 
strain or strss or pressure. In spite of 
all these efforts, some campers may 
appear to return home tired, but in 
this connection parents should keep in 
mind that this is often the natural 
reaction to a change of environment. 

Included in our consideration of 
health is the matter of cleanliness and 
tidiness. Camp stresses that a good 
camper lives cleanly and comfortably 
in his environment, both in camp and 
on out-trips. A good camper is clean 
and keeps clothes and possessions neat 
and tidy. By general consent, the 
“rough-tough” period of camping is 
over. However, parents understand the 
perpetual struggle that goes on to 
achieve cleanliness and tidiness and the 
tendency for some children not to be 
so clean and tidy as they might be. 
Camps do their best to meet this chal¬ 
lenge and to inculcate such ideals and 
habits. 

The camp’s second major responsi¬ 
bility is to do everything possible to 
provide able, trained, mature leader¬ 
ship, because it is leadership, more than 
anything else, that makes the camp. 
The group counsellor is at the very 
centre of the group’s camp experience. 
Everything else in camp, including 
other staff members, buildings and 
equipment, exist and are designed to 
assist the group counsellor in succeeding 
in this undertaking. In a very real 
sense, too, the director and senior staff' 
members work through the group coun¬ 
sellor. So much at camp is “caught” 
rather than “taught”; caught from 
counsellors’ ideas, attitudes, way of 


Toronto 9 Canada, April 1958 


119 



doing things, ideals and principles 
through day-by-day, or rather minute- 
by-minute contacts and associations. 
Often the counsellor’s leadership and 
influence is most felt when there is 
apparently nothing going on, in those 
in-between periods, when the counsel¬ 
lor’s real self shines through. Parents 
realize that there is great variation in 
human personality. Some counsellors 
are particularly strong in some aspects 
of leadership; others in other phases, 
but all should have a contribution to 
make. 

Gamp should provide suitable facili¬ 
ties, equipment and site, for satisfactory 
camp living and desirable activities. 
Camp sites are chosen with reference 
to all these requirements. The basic 
aim and ideal is to keep the idea of 
“camp” in camping, to make the camp 
“campy” in the best sense of that word, 
and this in the face of modern encroach¬ 
ments. This aim applies to buildings, 
living quarters and the general camp 
set-up in the realization that these and 
other factors can destroy the true camp 
atmosphere. 

This “campy” approach also applies 
to programme. Gamp should make 
available a- well-rounded programme 
but one that stresses those activities 
which are intrinsically of the out-of- 
doors and of camp, and in which the 
camper does not regularly engage at 
home. These truly camp activities in¬ 
clude swimming, camp craft, nature 
lore, fishing, boating, canoeing, water- 
safety, hikes and out-trips. Other activ¬ 
ities such as crafts, riding, shooting, 
archery, games, sailing, dramatics, 
photography, water-skiing, etc., can be 
made available to establish a point of 
interest, to widen interests, and for 
their carry-over value when the camper 
returns home. 

Interest should be at the heart and 
core of programme and activities, start¬ 


ing with known interests and moving 
into new fields of interest. Gamp 
should not be content to accept a 
camper’s interests just as they are, but 
should strive to expand and enlarge 
them by giving the camper the oppor¬ 
tunity to explore and try out new activ¬ 
ities. All this can be done using sound 
educational methods and techniques 
without involving bribes, threats and 
awards. 

The camper should also have full 
opportunity to develop basic camping 
skills, such as swimming and canoeing, 
and to become highly proficient in 
them. Camp should develop campers 
who are highly skillful in some activ¬ 
ities, particularly these basic ones, and 
reasonably skillful in others so that all 
campers can feel, with modest confi¬ 
dence, that they are skillful at some¬ 
thing. May we point out, though, that 
while proficiency in these skills is highly 
important and justifies and requires 
much practice and instruction, even 
more important are the so-called con¬ 
comitant learnings — the personality 
and character training that takes place 
while the instruction and practice are 
proceeding. It is very important for a 
camper to learn to be a good swimmer 
— it is even more important to learn 
to be fair, honest, industrious, friendly 
and modest in the process. 

Because interest is the basis of pro¬ 
gramme and activity, campers along 
with counsellors, should have a share 
planning programme and activities. 
Campers’ participation in planning 
based on their own interests leads to 
greater achievements and results. Regi¬ 
mentation and formal methods fre¬ 
quently destroy this interest. Gamp 
should mean a large degree of freedom 
and fun, a leisurely, care-free experi¬ 
ence in the out-of-doors without undue 
pressure and tensions that sometimes 
exist by necessity, perhaps, in other 


120 


Canadian Camping 



situations. Camp should be a holiday 
in the finest sense of the word, with a 
feeling of release, with opportunities to 
rest and relax, to do what you want to 
do when you want to do it, to renew 
energies. By giving the camper the 
opportunity to make choices and deci¬ 
sions, according to his capabilities, and 
to share in the planning of programme, 
along with counsellors and staff mem¬ 
bers, the camp is able to help the 
camper enjoy this feeling of freedom 
and of being an integral member of a 
group. This method also results in 
wider and more interested participation 
on the part of the camper and is an 
essential part of the growing up and 
maturing process of the camper. 

Camping should be an adventure in 
democracy. The camp is a self-contained 
community in which campers observe 
at close range and in small, understand¬ 
able dimensions the functioning of a 
democratic society with the inter¬ 
dependence of its members and its 
methods of operation. With this know¬ 
ledge of a democratic society in m’'ma¬ 
ture should come an understanding of 
larger societies, municipal, provincial, 
national and inter-national, along with 
their methods, privileges and obliga¬ 
tions. In a democratic society, the indi¬ 
vidual member has certain duties and 
responsibilities to the whole group. 
Since democracy is dedicated to the 
development of each individual in the 
group, each member must respect the 
personality and individualty of every 
other member. Each member must 
have a feeling of security in belonging 
to the group, in knowing that nothing 
will be done to harm or thwart indi¬ 
vidual personality. For that reason, 
the “horse-play”, “practical ioke” phase 
of camping is also over. Campers do 
not have fun at the expense of other 
campers. The natural inter-play of 
personality and the informal discipline 
of a group should be a leavening, chal¬ 


lenging, inspiring influence, not always, 
of course, without some unpleasantness. 
But this unpleasantness, under wise 
leadership can often be made the best 
influence for good. Children must be 
taught to meet a certain amount of 
unpleasantness, adversity, failure and 
difficulty in order to be better equipped 
to meet these as life develops. Camp 
should not only be a training in all that 
is easy, pleasant, and happy but a 
training in what is difficult, unpleasant 
and unhappy as well. 

The discipline of camp starts with 
informal group discipline, it should be 
carried on without show of anger or 
emotion by counsellors who are fair, 
impartial agents for seeing that the 
natural, logical results or consequences 
of behaviour always inevitably follow, 
whether good or bad, pleasant or un¬ 
pleasant. This involves explaining why 
the behaviour is acceptable or unac¬ 
ceptable, and agreeing on the natural, 
logical consequences. This type of dis¬ 
cipline leads to self-discipline, which 
is our ultimate goal. 

In a democratic society, the indi¬ 
vidual has the right to develop to the 
full extent of his or her capacities. 
Camp should enable the camper to 
develop in self-reliance and resource¬ 
fulness, in self-control, self-restraint, 
self-discipline, in initiative and enter¬ 
prise, in leadership ability and the 
ability to live amicably and construc¬ 
tively with others. These qualities 
should not only have meaning in the 
camp environment, but should carry 
over to the home environment for year- 
round living. These are the aims and 
purposes, the values and methods that 
invite and challenge campers, parents, 
directors and counsellors to work 
together for their fulfillment. 


Toronto, Canada, April 1958 


121 



By F. Wm. Halliday, Pioneer Section 
Director, Camp Chief Hector, 
Operated by the Calgary YMCA. 


WE TURNED 
TO THE MOUNTAINS 


This past summer, the Pioneer Sec¬ 
tion of Camp Chief Hector, undertook 
an experiment new in Canadian Camp¬ 
ing, by initiating a mountain climbing 
programme. 

Considering the waterways on the 
eastern edge of the Rockies to be un¬ 
suitable for extended canoe tripping — 
the conventional programme of pioneer 
camping — Hector turned to the moun¬ 
tains to satisfy the activity needs of 
its older boy’s section. 

Our objective was to supply an outlet 
for the adventurous drives of fourteen 
and fifteen year old boys, through which 
they would develop physically, mentally 
and spiritually. Climbing proved to he 
a successful means to achieve this three¬ 
fold aim. 

Our first consideration was safety. 
Members of the Alpine Club of Canada 
were consulted; rules and plans of in¬ 
struction were drawn up and the nec¬ 
essary ropes and equipment were 
purchased. After the counsellors and 
other members of the staff had gained 
thorough knowledge and practice, the 
new programme was ready to be tested. 

A day at “Rock School” — an educa¬ 
tional institution where classrooms are 
supplanted by cliffs, where books and 
rulers are replaced by boots and ropes, 
and where truancy is unknown — was 
the camper’s introduction to the pro¬ 
gramme. 

The “School” is situated a few miles 
from camp on a cliff used by the Alpine 
Club for similiar instruction. The cliff 
is unique in that it presents an elemen¬ 
tary example of almost every obstacle a 
climber will meet, as well as a view 
which seems to have been designed to 
delight and inspire the climber. 


Here at “Rock School”, such strange 
terms as traverse, belay and rappel were 
to become meaningful to the young ad¬ 
venturers as denoting essential Alpine 
techniques. Here the Pioneers were to 
learn the skills of co-ordinating strength 
and agility to meet the challenge of the 
mountains. Here, also, each boy was to 
develop his sense of responsibility and 
co-operation, while affirming and realiz¬ 
ing his capabilities and limitations. 

Initial instruction included an ex¬ 
planation of the rules and methods of 
rock climbing, and of the use and care 
of the equipment. The belay, or means 
of safeguarding a fellow camper with 
the rope, was most highly emphasized 
at this point. Although nothing dan¬ 
gerous was ever undertaken in our 
climbing programme, the importance of 
every possible safety precaution was 
strongly impressed upon the mind of 
each camper. The overly courageous 
were to learn the values of common 
sense, and the timid were to gain the 
required confidence. 

Next on the “curriculum” came the 
practical instruction. This was under¬ 
taken in small groups under the direc¬ 
tion of the counsellors. Following their 
examples, and secured by their belays, 
each camper, increasing in skill and 
confidence with each attempt, practised 
the chimney, the vertical wall, and the 
traverse. 

Seated around the campfire at lunch¬ 
time, the Pioneers excitedly discussed 
their experiences, nonchalantly mispro¬ 
nouncing European climbing terms. It 
became obvious to the members of the 
staff that the new programme was pro¬ 
viding the desired emotional appeal.

By F. M. Van Wagner, President , 
Canadian Camping Association. 


TRY A TREE FARM 


Conservation of our wild life re¬ 
sources is so essential to our future 
happiness and prosperity that a con¬ 
tinuous educational campaign must be 
waged in its support. 

Camping people often consider what 
they can do in the interest of this cause. 
One project which a number of camps 
are carrying out, and which others 
could probably do something about, is 
reforestation. Cutting as well as plant¬ 
ing may be indicated in some instances. 
Other camps like ours may have cleared 
areas where solid stands could be 
planted, but in most cases, it would 
very likely be a case of scattering trees 
where space and conditions permit. 

One programme we feel to be worth¬ 
while, and not difficult to carry out, 
is to see that we have growing on camp 
property, where they can be seen, a 
few specimens of every species of tree 
indigenous to our region. A fair number 
of these trees should have name markers 
for easy identification. 

Unfortunately, the best time for 
planting is earlv spring, soon after the 
frost is out of the ground, when most 
campers are unable to participate. 
However, with care, a limited amount 
of planting can be done during the 
camp season. 

The following is a brief report of 
what is being done to develop a tree 
farm at Camp Nominingue. We have 
available for this purpose seventy-five 
to one hundred acres of sandy soil that 
was cleared many years ago, and on 



which there is now a very sparse growth 
of poplar and pin cherry. 

During the past eight years, twenty 
thousand trees have been planted, most¬ 
ly in solid stands at about seven foot 
spacing. This gives about nine hundred 
trees per acre. 

The following species have been 
planted: red pine, jack pine, Scotch 
pine, white spruce, Norway spruce, 
European larch and a few red oak. 
White cedar have also been planted, 
but where there is more moisture. 

The planting is done by counsellors 
and senior campers on the first week¬ 
end of May each year. The pines do 
best when set where there is no cover. 
The sod is removed and the plant set 
in exposed sand. At least 95% survive. 
On the other hand, spruce require a 
light cover for the first few years. The 
Scotch and jack pines grow most rapid¬ 
ly, some reaching over six feet in five 
years. The Scotch pines, of course, make 
excellent Christmas trees if you wish to 
cut them. 

Our tree farm has now reached the 
stage where campers show quite an 
interest in our reforestation project. 
This, of course, we are most anxious to 
encourage. 

The Quebec Department of Lands 
and Forests provides the plants, we pay 
only packing and express charges. Be¬ 
fore supplying trees, a Department rep¬ 
resentative visited camp to determine 
what kind of trees were best suited for 
continued on page 150 


Toronto , Canada , April. 1958 


125 




There is no group in camping today 
that would suggest seriously that we 
need not train our camp staffs. There 
are, however, differences of opinion 
about what we mean by training, and 
even more diversity around our train¬ 
ing objectives. 

As I observe the scene, most camps 
engage in some form of pre-camp train¬ 
ing, and let it go at that. 

From time to time groups in the 
Camping Association have tried to 
evaluate the effectiveness of pre-camp 
counsellor training. In most of the 
instances studied, the demonstrated re¬ 
sults of pre-camp counsellor training 
have been disappointing, to say the 
least, and yet we persist in relying 
upon it almost wholly for our training 


We should be quite clear, however, 
that while the above mentioned results 
are part of over-all training objectives, 
they are not the real training goals. 
The goals I have in mind are related 
to the manner in which a counsellor 
handles himself on the job. You may 
call this leadership training, or training 
in working with children. If these are 
our basic goals, pre-camp training is 
not the most effective method for 
achieving them. It is for this reason 
that I venture to oppose the trend and 
suggest that we undertake to do what 
we can do well, and use our time and 
methods with more discrimination. By 
this I mean that we teach programme 
skills in pre-camp training because we 
can, and because counsellors need to 


SOME SUGGESTED TRAINING TECHNIQUES 

By Alan F. Klein 


programmes. Looking at it realistical¬ 
ly, pre-camp training does serve many 
useful functions. For some camps it 
accomplishes the work necessary for 
opening camp, and in so doing helps 
the staff members to become familiar 
and comfortable with the camp en¬ 
vironment and equipment. It settles 
them into camp life. Even more im¬ 
portant, if well done, it fuses the staff 
into a group and sets the atmosphere 
for loyalty and team spirit. Budget- 
wise camp directors must equate these 
results with the cost of a pre-camp 
week on site. It is expensive business. 
Some might find that these results can 
be obtained in a shorter period of time 
if designed differently or that it could 
be done by combining pre-camp in-the- 
city meetings with a pre-camp week¬ 
end on the site. 


have activity skills if they are to be 
effective. Leadership skill is of para¬ 
mount importance, to be sure, but 
without camp activity skill, the coun¬ 
sellor is operating in the dark without 
the slightest idea of how to turn the 
lights on. Some may go through the 
entire summer in this state. 

The art and skill of working with 
children is best learned and hence 
taught on the job. This can be accom¬ 
plished through supervision and train¬ 
ing sessions with small homogeneous 
groups of counsellors. Supervision is .an 
educational process through which a 
person who knows more teaches some 
one who knows less on a face-to-face 
basis. The prime factor is that the 
Learner be helped to solve his own 
problems as they arise on the job. 
Learning is achieved when the learner 


126 


Canadian Camping 





is active and is engaged in solving prob¬ 
lems that have meaning to him or to 
her. For this reason, on the job learn¬ 
ing is faster and more effective than 
pre-camp learning. 

We have said that supervision is one 
of the most effective methods of train¬ 
ing. However, here also, I must risk 
censure and go contrary to the trend. 
This method has not been successful 
in many camps because a long time 
back someone sold us on the unit 
system. Unit or section heads were 
to supervise the counsellors. The idea 
is sound administratively. Decentrali¬ 
zation has many advantages but, in 
reality, supervision is not one of them 
because most of us can not obtain 
unit heads who are qualified to super¬ 
vise, either because we can not afford 
them or because they do not exist. It 
is said that if you wish to teach a dog 
some tricks you must know more than 
the dog does. Many unit heads do not 
know substantially more than the coun¬ 
sellors do, nor are they more mature; 
and secondly, they do not know how to 
supervise, which is a specific training 
skill. Consequently, we adopted an 
administrative structure and have re¬ 
lied upon it in many settings in spite 
of the fact that we have not been able 
to secure personnel appropriate to the 
structure to make it run at a high level 
of efficiency from a training point of 
view. I think I would prefer to employ 
one senior supervisor, charged with 
the responsibility of staff training, keep 
the decentralized plan by using a senior 
counsellor as my unit co-ordinator, and 
give up the idea of unit heads super¬ 
vising staff'. 

In the last few years some new ideas 
have been developed in training and 
have proven themselves in industry and 
adult education. They might be used 
in pre-camp training or during the 
camp season. Those that I will men¬ 


tion all depend upon a few fundamen¬ 
tal training principles: 

1. Only the counsellor can change 
his own performance. He must, 
therefore, be involved actively in the 
training process. 

2. Adults learn more readily 
through problem-solving exercises. 

3. Learning is accelerated if the 
problems discussed are significant to 
the learner. 

4. Aimless discussion is frustrating. 
There must be guidance and direc¬ 
tion by the trainer. 

5. Human relations skills require 
insight into one’s own way of 
working. 

6. The learners must want to learn 
and change. 

7. All learning is accompanied by 
resistance to learning which is in¬ 
tensified by threat or fear. 

8. Effective learning requires the 
support of a small friendly group of 
colleagues. 

These principles imply that all our 
personnel are committed to a common 
goal, and that the goal is made explicit. 
They imply also that the staff members 
experience satisfaction of their own 
personal needs. That means good in¬ 
terpersonal relationships; status given 
for doing a good job with campers and 
not for looks, apple polishing, athletic 
skill and so on; an atmosphere condu¬ 
cive to learning, with rewards based 
upon satisfaction from doing a good 
job accompanied by encouragement 
and praise; and an opportunity for 
shared leadership in a democratic 
setting. 

To summarize, then, the principles 
of all such training require that the 
learner have access to ideas, attitude 
and modes of behavior alternative to 
the ones he possesses; there must be a 
setting in which he can examine and 
test new ways; and he needs support

Western Leckie Limited

and social success in experimenting 
with new forms of behavior before he 
can adopt them as his own. 

To clarify terms and concepts let us 
observe that training connotes ‘how to 
do a job” white education means some¬ 
thing broader. Here we are talking 
about training counsellors for a job. 

While we are clarifying, let us settle 
another question. Do our words so far 
mean that one may never lecture to 
counsellors? They do not. When the 
content consists of facts, procedures, 
and non-debatable material it can be 
given as a lecture or in a written man¬ 
ual. It is more useful and acceptable 
and therefore learned more quickly 
when the learner wants and needs the 
information, but we are not throwing 
the “telling” method out completely. 

The methods that follow will be de¬ 
scribed very briefly since each could be 
profitably the subject of an article by 
itself. *>< 

Role Playing 

This is a training method that is 
both powerful^ and effective. In it the 
learning situation is enacted and meth¬ 
ods of handling oneself in the situation 
are tried and evaluated and then the 
new insights are tested. It has been 
abused by charlatans who have thought 
that all there was to it was to put on 
a dramatic skit. In fact, it is a sensi¬ 
tive training tool and should be studied 
hefore attempting to use it. It is ad¬ 
mirably suited to camp training. 

Case Study 

In this method a detailed narrative 
of a situation is given. The whole case 
is described. The trainees are asked to 
analyze what happened, to explain the 
behaviour of the campers, to critically 
examine the work of the counsellor l and 
to suggest alternate ways of approach¬ 
ing the problem. 

The case might present a problem 
without revealing the counsellors ac¬ 
tion and the trainees may be asked 
what they would do. Alternate sugges- 


128 


Canadian Camping 










tions are examined and consequences 
explored. In this method, principles 
must be drawn from the discussion. 
Gamp policy, procedures and routines 
can be taught at the same time from 
the same case. The cases are written 
from your own camp records and 
experiences. 

The Incident Method 

In this method, instead of giving a 
complete case, one sentence describing 
an incident is given. For example, 
“When the cabin group left for the 
council ring Joel refused to go, saying 
that he was tired.” The trainees must 
ask questions of the person who knows 
the full story. This might be a more 
experienced counsellor. The value of 
this method is that it helps the trainees 
to develop a questioning approach to 
situations, they learn what questions to 
ask and what to look for, and they get 
the information they want to know and 
not what we want to tell them. When 
they try to solve the problem they may 
find that they have not learned enough 
facts. This develops motivation to 
learn more. 

The trainee is stimulated to try to get 
his bearings in the situation. He must 
get the facts and then sort out the key 
facts. He must determine what the 
question is in the incident. 

After many questions have been 
asked and facts gleaned, the trainees 
are encouraged to summarize the situa¬ 
tion. Then everyone is asked to write 
what he believes to be the real ques¬ 
tion, a solution and his reasons, in ten 
minutes. This prevents many from sit¬ 
ting back letting a few do the thinking 
and work. 

Improved staff means improved per¬ 
formance, and better camping. Camp 
management has not kept up with the 
trend in other enterprises to improve 
and increase personnel training. It is 
good business and pays many different 
kinds of dividends.

By Dorothy M. Douglas 


TWO PROJECTS FOR YOUR CAMPERS 


OPEN A WINDOW ON THE 
WORLD 

Here are two types of project for 
your campers this summer which will 
fill many hours with absorbing activity, 
and which can lead to rewarding re¬ 
sults both for those campers who parti¬ 
cipate and for those less fortunate and 
needy children in other parts of the 
world. 

HI NEIGHBOUR! Folklore 
Activities Kit 

Prepared by UNICEF, the United 
Nations International Children’s Emer¬ 
gency Fund, and available for $1 from 
their Canadian office at 280 Bloor St. 
West, Toronto, this colourful kit of 
booklets and posters includes projects 
for large and small groups. It can be 
used on the playground, in camps, or 
classrooms. Offering a programme to 
broaden the horizons of school-age 
children, the kit outlines games, songs, 
crafts, and dances of five countries. The 
1957 kit contains Iraq, The Philippines, 
Guatemala, Nigeria, and Yugoslavia. 


For 1958, the kit is in the form of a 
sixty-four page book on Italy, Indo¬ 
nesia, Lebanon, Paraguay and Uganda. 

HI NEIGHBOUR! Companion 
Recording 

A ten-inch Long Playing Recording, 
prepared to supplement the kit, con¬ 
tains songs on one side and dances on 
the other, one each from the five 
countries of the kit. (Words and music 
are in the kit.) We did not expect to 
find this music so delightful; it is very 
rhythmical, with light drums, pipes and 
sometimes marimba-like instruments. 
The music of Guatemala and The 
Philippines is particularly enchanting, 
perhaps, for Western ears. The record 
costs $3. Both record and kit may be 
obtained from CANADIAN UNICEF 
COMMITTEE, 280 Bloor St. West, 
Toronto 5, Ontario. 

As you may know, UNICEF is the 
world’s largest international effort to 
improve the health and welfare of 
children and the mothers who bear 
them. Its programme is three-fold: 


130 


Canadian Camping 



mass disease control, maternal and 
child welfare, and nutrition. UNICEF 
aid requires self-help and so the assisted 
countries spend $2 for every $1 con¬ 
tributed by the Fund. It is reaching 
forty-five million mothers and children 
in ninety-five countries. To show the 
children here what their pennies can do 
to help, one leaflet tells us that the 
pennies you spend on a comic book will 
give a child fifty glasses of milk in 
India, for an ice-cream cone, ten child¬ 
ren can receive protection from T.B. 
in Chile, for a candy bar a child can 
be cured of the horrible sores of yaws 
in Nigeria. Whether, with the ideas 
and materials mentioned above, we 
“open a window on the world” so that 
our campers become interested and 
ready to explore further, or whether 
through a money-raising project, we 
encourage them to spread “a rainbow 
around the world” (one of UNICEF’s 
catchy songs) we will be launching a 
worthwhile venture. All materials are 
generously illustrated with photographs 
and drawings. 

UNESCO AND YOUTH 
Information Kit, Programme Aids 

The United Nations Educational, 
Scientific, and Cultural Organization 
offers a plan of youth education for 
social responsibility and international 
co-operation and opens up a tremen¬ 
dous field of interest. Their projects 
are geared to high school and college 
young people, those who are senior 
campers and young counsellors, for 
whom an Information Kit has been 
prepared with materials helpful to 
group leaders, teachers, and speakers. 
Ask for their “Attention Committee 
Chairman” folder which lists 16mm 
films, filmstrips, dramatic scripts for 
one-act plays, posters and pamphlets 
about UNESCO. 

To us in the Western world who take 
free education for granted, it is dis- 

continned on page 133

TREASURY OF AMERICAN 
INDIAN TALES 

Theodore Whitson Ressler. 

Forty-four authentic Indian Tales, 
each one short enough to hold the 
interest of campers at a gathering under 
the trees, or at the campfire — such a 
collection is precious to the counsellor 
of a group between 6 and 12 years of 
age. The style is dramatic, but the 
vocabularly simple enough that the 
older pre-teen campers could read them 
aloud. The tales are grouped into in¬ 
terest areas of Adventure, Heroism, 
Customs, Character, Hunting and Fish¬ 
ing, among some of which such values 
as courage, truthfulness, sound family 
relationships are quite effectively con¬ 
veyed. 

Mr. Ressler is a Y.M.C.A. worker 
who has also been active with the Boy 
Scouts for many years, among whom, he 


has developed a reputation as a teller 
of tales. He has made a life-long hobby 
of collecting Indian stories, many of 
which have been related to him by 
personal Indian friends. G. R. Welch 
Co. Ltd. Toronto. $4.25. 

INDIAN COUNCIL RING 

W. J. Eastaugh. 

Recognized as a leading authority on 
Indian Lore, the traditions of the In¬ 
dian Council Ring and the organiza¬ 
tion of effective Indian ceremonies, Mr. 
Jack Eastaugh has compiled a forty- 
four page booklet containing detailed 
instructions concerning this type of pro¬ 
gramme for camp use. As each step is 
outlined, charts make clear the council 
ring, illustrations show details of ac¬ 
cessories and give instructions on how 
to make them, simply and economically. 
Articles of clothing can be made, simply 
by studying the drawings; an effective 
headband appears on one page, various 
parts of an Indian costume on others; 
tribe names are explained; totems suit¬ 
able for cabin groups are illustrated, 
and a number of ceremonies outlined. 
One page in particular will be enjoyed 
by campers ... it tells how to make 
scalps! 

“The supply of books is quite limit¬ 
ed”, says Mr. Eastaugh, “until such 
time as it is practical to go into print. If 
you would like to purchase your copy 
now, the price is $2. Please enclose 
purchase price with your order and 
send it to W. J. Eastaugh, 5 Beatty 
Avenue, Brampton, Ontario. 

—E. F.

stock, to stand back and get the long

THE SUCCESSFUL CAMP 

Lewis C. Reimann. 

To answer the needs of new camp 
directors and to supplement the knowl¬ 
edge gained through experience by 
those who have been in camping over 
the years, Mr. Reimann writes of the 
basic organization of a camp from the 
selection of the site itself to the last 
record of evaluation after camp is over 
for the year. For the collection of 
sample forms and applications alone, 
The Successful Camp is a valuable 
book to include in the camp directors 
library . . . Camp Staff Application, 
Leadership Information Form, Em¬ 
ployee Release, Camper Application for 


134 


Canadian Camping 




Enrolment, Camper Personality Ques¬ 
tionnaire, Camper Equipment Check 
List, Health Examination Form, Daily 
Camp Schedule, Camper Behaviour 
Chart, Counsellor’s Final Report on 
Campers, and Camp Evaluation . . . 
they are all here for other directors to 
use and to copy. 

Mr. Reimann discusses standards and 
programme, purchasing and financing,

WILD LIFE CORNER 


One day this coming summer, why 
not stand astride a large, bold outcrop¬ 
ping of rock, the sort of thing found 
around most camps? Try to project 
your imagination back countless mil¬ 
lions of years to a time when the whole 
earth was composed of nothing but 
silent, barren rock, with restless seas 
pounding upon it. The rocks, the seas, 
the sun . . . from these the world began. 

The seas rose and washed over the 
rocks. Winds and rains chiselled them, 
washing the particles ever down to the 
seas. There were cataclysmic eruptions, 
heavings, shifts and settlings of the 
earth’s crust, but no one saw or heard 
these changes. 

It is almost impossible to conceive 
of these things, and yet, to try is to 
grasp the deep mystery, the awesome¬ 
ness of the world in which we live. 
Does your nature programme convey 
this awe and mystery to the campers? 

What miracle produced life on these 
barren rocks? It was a miracle; not the 
thunder-clapping kind that we have in 
mind, but a painfully slow type of 
miracle that can be observed as still 
going on in our own camps today. 

We need not wait millions of years 
for the various forms of plant life to 
evolve. The time cycle has been tele¬ 
scoped, but the original pattern is there. 
Dr. William Gunn has described this 
phenomena so simply and clearly in 
his booklet “Nature Study”, that his 
words are repeated here: 

“On this boulder (or rock out-crop), 
you can see that there are some very 
small, flat green and grey plants grow¬ 


By Barry G. Lowes, Director, 
Camp Timberlane. 


ing. These are called lichens (pro¬ 
nounced likens) and they are particu¬ 
larly interesting because they can grow 
on bare rock where other plants cannot 
grow. They are also interesting because 
they are examples of the first stages of 
a series of events, taking a long, long 
time, that must take place before a 
big forest of tall trees can grow. 

“These lichens are able to live on 
water and sunlight and certain very 
small amounts of chemicals they are 
able to extract from the rock. As the 
lichens live and die, their remains 
gradually add up to form little bits of 
soil that mingle with tiny bits of rock 
broken up by wind and rain and frost 
and by the action of the plants. 

“After a while, there comes a time 
when enough soil has been created so 
that mosses can grow here ... as you 
can see has happened on this spot over 
here. Many generations of mosses live 
and die in turn, and their remains 
gradually form quite a thick pad of soil 
that eventually is able to support some 
of the hardiest kinds of grasses. 

“Soon, as you can see here, other 
grasses and sedges take over and they 
make a still thicker layer of nourishing 
top-soil. 

“In this part of the country, where 
the climate is best suited for the growth 
of forests, rather than grasses, other 
plants are then able to take over from 
the grasses and sedges. Young trees 
come up from seed, and such trees as 
poplar, hawthorn and cherry spring 
up, soon cutting out the sunlight from 
the smaller plants. That is the sort of 
thing that is going on right now over 
there where those young poplars are. 


136 


Canadian Camping 



“Eventually^ those trees in turn give 
way to maple, beech or oak and elm 
trees, such as you can see in that 
woodlot over there. They represent the 
last stage in the long sequence, because 
young maples and beeches are able to 
grow successfully under the shade of 
adult trees. And so the young trees in 
time, take over from the older ones, 
all the while adding to the soil beneath. 

“This business of plant succession is 
going on around us all the time. The 
settlers and farmers have changed the 
stages of the natural succession in many 
places, but if the land were again left 
to itself, it would go back into forest. 

“This type of succession is called 
‘dry succession’ because it begins with 
plants growing on dry rock. There is 
another kind called ‘wet succession’ that 
we will talk about next. 

WET SUCCESSION 

“Here, by this pond, is a place where 
you can see an example of ‘wet’ 
succession. 

“Let’s begin out in the middle of the 
pond, where it is quite deep. Floating 
around in the water, out there, are 
many extremely small plants called 
algae. They are so small that you would 
need a microscope to see them. But 
collectively they add up to quite a lot 
. . . enough, sometimes, to give the 
water a greenish or blue-ish colour. 

“These algae either sink to the bot¬ 
tom when they die, or they are eaten 
by small animals that, in turn, contri¬ 
bute to forming a bottom soil in which 
other plants can grow. 

“As we move shore wards from the 
deep water, the first new plants we 
come across are those that can grow 
entirely underwater without emerging 
into the air. These are the true aquatic 
plants. You can sometimes see these by 


looking down into the water from a 
boat. They do need some sunlight 
though, and cannot grow where the 
water is too deep. As these plants live 
and die, their remains tend to build 
up the bottom soil and thus the pond 
gets shallower and shallower. Soon we 
reach a point where the water is shallow 
enough that the plants like water lilies 
and pond lilies can have their roots in 
the bottom and still have their leaves 
and flowers above the water, in the air. 

“Over a long period of time, these 
plants, in turn, add layers to the 
bottom, always tending to make the 
pond shallower. Soon we reach a stage 
of shallowness where first rushes and 
then cat-tail reeds can grow out of the 
water, just as you see them there. 

As the water-level drops to a few 
inches, sedges . . . such as these, here . . . 
do very well in wet or moist soil. They 
bridge the crossing from water to land 
and then the grasses come in ... as you 
can see here. And from this stage, the 
plant succession follows the same route 
that we saw in ‘dry’ succession, ending 
up the same way with a forest of tall 
trees. 

“In ‘wet’ succession, the general ten¬ 
dency is for all the plants growing in 
the water to add to the bottom layer of 
soil so that the pond becomes shallower 
all the time. Eventually it may become 
a bog in which trees can get a foothold, 
and the forest takes over. That is a 
long, slow process. But you may see 
bogs with trees such as tamaracks in 
them in which this process is going on.” 

We cannot all be Dr. Gunns, nor 
can we have him on our staff, but 
every one of us from director to junior 
counsellor can be curious, can experi¬ 
ence the excitement of discovery, the 
beauty of balance and harmony, _ the 
awe and mystery, as we contemplate 

continued on page 138

these phenomena in progress. Once we 
feel it, we must convey it to the 
campers. 

In place of a formal “nature pro¬ 
gramme”, let’s strive to develop in our 
campers a heightened awareness of the 
world about them that becomes an in¬ 
tegral part of their every waking hour, 
from the mist-shrouded lake at sunrise, 
to the infinite depths of the sky at night; 
from the single-celled animals found in 
swamp water to the deer and bear of 
the forests. 

Their eyes (and ours) will be opened 
to a new conception of the world, and 
their own place in it will take on new 
meaning. 

Too difficult an assignment? Not 
really. The materials sire all about us. 
The only equipment needed is an uiY- 
bridled curiosity which sets all our 
senses free.

sunsets, and I hear the campers sing¬ 
ing — 

“Unto the hills around do I 
lift up mine eyes” 

“Day is dying in the west” 

It was Star Night. A University Pro¬ 
fessor had given a talk on “The Stars”. 
By the embers of the camp fire, the 
boys looked up and listened for an 
hour or more. Then one boy quietly 
said, “Now I know the meaning of the 
first words of the Bible, “In the begin¬ 
ning, God”. We were as pebbles on an 
endless shore by the Sea of Infinity. 
“He made the stars also”. 

At each camp, we chose one great 
picture from the inspired Masters. It 
was placed over the fireplace through¬ 
out the camp and we studied it and 
loved it. One year we chose Watt’s “Sir 
Galahad” in Eton College Chapel, and 
we prayed — “My Lord, I am ready 
on the threshold of this new day to go 
forth armed with Thy power. Grant, at 
the end of the day no blot may be 


found on my Shield. Amen.” 

For each camp, we chose a great 
Musician. We learned of his life and 
his inspired genius. God inspired him, 
i.e. — God breathed into him the im¬ 
mortal music. By our Music Director 
and by recordings, we became acquaint¬ 
ed with some of his deathless melodies. 
We were imbued with “an awareness 
of the Eternal”. We were worshipping 
God. 

From the hikes, we brought back 
flowers and mounted them; we learned 
their names and admired their beauty. 
From the flower crannied in the wall, 
we were near to God. 

The fire burned low. “Silently, one 
by one, in the infinite meadows of 
heaven, blossomed the lovely stars, the 
forget-me-nots of the angels”. 

Then we sang — 

“God who touchest earth with beauty, 

Make my heart anew; 

Keep me ever by Thy Spirit, 

Pure, and strong, and true”.

PRESERVE AND SAVE . . . 


A good preservative for wood and canvas is among the Absolute Necessities 
of camp supplies, and we have been gleaning one or two interesting facts about 
Cuprinol, during the last little while, which camp directors should know. 

Probably one of the most important trom the safety standpoint is that it is 
harmless to clothing and skin, a point to consider when workmen come into the 
maintenance picture. They, too, will appreciate the ease with which it can be 
applied by merely dipping the item to be treated, or by using brush or spray. 

What a good many of us don’t realize, however, is that protection can be 
assured with one coat of Guprinol without changing the character of the wood. 
Yacht and Boat Builders use it for treating new wood before it goes into the 
craft. Greenhouse owners use it without damage to plants. Wood for ties and 
bridges have been treated with it extensively. And down Boston way, Douglas 
Fir lobster tanks were treated with Clear Guprinol to produce a tank which 
would be free from all algae marine growth and worms. 

A product that gives absolute protection against rot and mildew, one that 
will stop rot already started, is a good one to have on hand, with spring main¬ 
tenance days facing us. Equipment protected is equipment saved.

ALBERTA CAMPING ASSOCIATION WORKSHOP 
held February 28th - March 2nd, 1958 


A representative group from the membership of the Alberta Camping 
As ocation met at Calgary for these three days to hold intensive discussions on 
the following topics: 

Campsite management and planning. 

Programme planning techniques. 

Staff training. 

Health and safety. 

Among the group of 28 persons registered, were representatives from the 
Boy Scouts, Girl Guides, Y.M.C.A., and a number of church camping groups. 
Geographically, the members of the workshop came from as far north as 
Edmonton and as far south as Lethbridge. 

The Workshop Committee under the chairmanship of Mr. N. Gamble, 
arranged for Mr. W. E. (Ted) Yard from Toronto to come as the director of 
the workshop. 

The Alberta Camping Association will be holding its annual conference in 
Edmonton this year. The training workshop was an additional project of this 
active Association.
