WILL THIS 

Interest Your Campers? 


By G. C. Toner, 
Royal Ontario Museum. 


Always there is room in the camp 
programme, perhaps around the camp¬ 
fire, or at the dinner table, for reliable 
information about the flora and fauna 
of the rural area about us. Mr. Toner 
has been writing for some years on 
just such topics, many of which have 
appeared in the Bancroft Times. Can¬ 
adian Camping has been given permis¬ 
sion to reprint a collection of his 
tid-bits, for their extreme value to the 
camp directors and staff members . . . 
all of us who sometimes find it difficult 
•to put our fingers on this kind of infor¬ 
mation. Why not clip these stories and 
paste them in that looseleaf memo book 
we should be preparing now for sum¬ 
mer use? 

Wood In The Far North 

Wood is rare and precious in Ontario’s 
far north. Birch does not grow within 
a hundred miles of southern Hudson 
Bay, nor does any other hardwood, 
save poplar, and the only source of 
wood fit for replacing broken axe 
handles, fixing canoes, etc., is the rivers 
which reach into interior Canada and 
bring it down to be deposited on the 
beach. 


In an arresting commentary on “The 
Worth of Wood” in the current issue 
of SYLVA, the bi-monthly magazine of 
the Ontario Department of Lands and 
Forests, J. A. Macfie, conservation and 
wildlife management officer here, says: 

“As Philip Mathew, my Cree Indian 
companion, and I hurried along the 
crest of the high, wide beach toward 
our tent and supper, we occasionally 
paused to pick up bits of dry, sound 
looking driftwood for the evening fire. 
The beach was the northern fringe of 
Ontario near where the Niskibi River 
empties into Hudson Bay and as it is 
over most of its length, the high tide 
mark was delineated by a tangle of 
driftwood; the roots, limbs and the 
entire trees, the dock timbers, railway 
ties and broken paddles spewed out into 
the Bay each spring by rivers draining 
a quarter of Canada’s surface. 

“Suddenly Philip dropped his armful 
of spruce firewood leaped into the wind¬ 
row and withdrew a four-foot length of 
wood which I recognized by a fragment 
of clinging mark as a chunk of white 
birch that had escaped from a beaver 
dam far up some river. 


142 


Canadian Camping 



“Before hoisting the stick to his 
shoulder to carry it to camp, he told 
me it was ‘minawsin atik’, a good tree. 
By way of explanation, he pointed to 
the handle of the axe I carried. He also 
tore off* a brittle curl of bark and put it 
in his pocket for tinder for some future 
campfire. 

“Since Philip has never in his 40 
years been inland beyond the great 
muskeg, he has never seen birch grow¬ 
ing. He only knows it as a sun and 
salt-whitened article that occurs rarely 
among the spruce, poplar and willow 
driftwood lining the beaches east and 
west of his native Fort Severn. 

“A few days later, we were walking 
a raised beach ridge where shore ice 
of receding Hudson Bay once piled up 
gravel, then abandoned it for a new 
beach 200 yards to seaward. The drift¬ 
wood there was old; spruce roots were 
nothing but hollow shells, though ap¬ 
pearing sound on the outside. 

“Among these ghosts of tree roots 
lay a harsher form, a short piece of 
12 by 12 inch square timber with corners 
sharp and scarcely weathered after 
decades in the dry sand. Philip demon¬ 
strated on the quality of this exotic bit 
by nipping off a comer with his knife, 
revealing the hardness and distinctive 
grain of oak, and describing it as 
‘muskwa’ (strong) wood. 

“He told me of the virtues of oak in 
the same way he explained where geese 
nest, and that caribou tracks disappear¬ 
ing under the tide are made by animals 
going out to feed on rockweed—things 
which are peculiar to his part of Ontario. 

“I didn’t tell Philip that I was fam¬ 
iliar with oak, and how it grew with 
great spreading branches and a trunk 
thicker and taller than he had ever 
seen. I am not sure he ever wonders 
where this wood originates. All that

concerns him is that oak comes in the 
form of timbers from old ships and 
staves from long disentigrated pork 
barrels, and it is the best material for 
repairing toboggans and strengthening 
canoe thwarts that the factories never 
make strong enough to withstand the 
bouncing weight of a seated man when 
Hudson Bay is rough. 

“The timber was too big to carry, 
but no doubt Philip steered his dogs 
that way the next winter, pried the 
block from the shallow snow and took 
it to his winter camp a few miles inland. 

“Philip’s people and the men of the 
Fludson’s Bay Company posts on this 
coast have long coveted wood from the 
south. When Radisson was at Port 
Nelson in the late 1600’s, he offered to 
trade rolls of birch bark brought from 
the bottom of James Bay. A hundred 
years later, birch wood for snowshoe 


frames was sent north to Fort Severn 
from Moose Factory on the sloop which 
distributed provisions and trade goods 
brought by ship from England. 

“Several times during the remaining 
long evening of our trip, Philip removed 
the precious billet of birch from the 
bottom of the canoe where it tempor¬ 
arily helped separate baggage and bilge- 
water to admire and work on it. 

“He whittled away all the hard brown 
underbark overlooked by the beaver and 
trimmed off the ragged end caused 
when tree separated from stump—the 
stump left imprisoned in the bank of 
an unknown stream high in the head¬ 
waters of the Nelson or the Churchill, 
the Severn or the Weisk, while the trunk 
rode an ever-broadening current down 
to a world where man regards white 
birch not as a valueless species but as 
‘minawson atik”, a good tree.”

How the Ontario Association 
for Retarded Children piloted 


A CAMP F0RTHESERI0U8LY RETARDED 


By John N. Haddad, Director, 

Camp Scugog South; Chairman, 

Recreation Committee , Ontario Association 
for Retarded Children. 


For centuries, seriously retarded 
children have been denied the most 
elementary educational and recreational 
experiences. These are the children who 
are still not allowed into our public 
education system because their I.Q. is 
below 50. Of all handicapped groups, 
the mentally retarded form a relatively 
large percentage of the population. It 
is generally agreed that thirty out of 
each thousand people are retarded to 
some extent. Because this condition is 
an incidence of population, the break¬ 
down of this group of thirty is known. 
Of this thirty, one is totally dependent, 
probably requiring care in an institu¬ 
tion. At the other end of the scale, 
twenty-five of the thirty are educable, 
most likely able to support themselves. 
The remaining group of four of each 
thirty are the seriously retarded child¬ 
ren, trainable to some degree, but who 
probably can never be completely inde¬ 
pendent. Besides being intellectually 
less endowed, many of these children 
have distinctive physical characteristics 
such as mongolism, or other physical 
handicaps due to disease or injury prior, 
during, or after being born. 

The Guelph Kiwanis Camp at Lake 
Belwood, near Fergus, Ontario is the 


first Canadian camp to experiment with 
a programme for these children. For 
two years, a man of vision, the Rev¬ 
erend Walter McLeary, who founded 
the camp, carried on a programme 
when no one else would. This last year, 
the Ontario Association for Retarded 
Children was approached to sponsor 
the camp. This is a province-wide or¬ 
ganization, so the camp began to reflect 
this. Campers, counsellors, and the com¬ 
mittee of OARC responsible for the 
camp were recruited from the entire 
province. We had no funds to hire any 
professional pre-camp staff* but one of 
our energetic volunteers, June Braaten, 
was in on the planning from the begin¬ 
ning. Without her devoted service and 
experience with both recreation and 
retarded children, the camp would 
never have been the success it was. 

Last year’s programme was designed 
as a pilot project experiment. We 
wanted to run a camp with a high 
standard of quality. We wanted to get 
the answers, at least in part, to a host 
of questions. What kind of physical 
plant and campsite do we need for 
these children? How can camping bene¬ 
fit them? What kind of training do the 
counsellors require? Which of the

We decided on an experimental ratio 
of one counsellor to every three camp¬

of learning to swim, the children re¬ 
quired individual instruction, a ratio of 
one adult to each child. This experi¬ 
mental ratio worked out well, generally 
speaking, but we would have been able 
to keep one lad who was sent home, if 
we had arranged for him to have his 
own counsellor. Counting cooks, special¬ 
ists and administrative staff, the overall 
ratio was one adult to every two camp¬ 
ers. In order to allow for time off and 
the individual attention that is neces¬ 
sary, the ratio cannot be larger than 
this. 

In spite of the fact that many of 
these children had not been separated 
from their home for even a week-end, 
we found there was no more homesick¬ 
ness than in a camp for normal child¬ 
ren. This is a most encouraging finding, 
since some parents felt the length of 
stay at camp should only be a week. We 
had decided upon a three week period 
and, although our research findings are 
not fully tabulated, there is some evi¬ 
dence that if the period had ended after 
two weeks, many personal, social and 
educational gains would probably have 
been lost, since improvement levels were 
generally highest during the third week. 

Most regular camping activities, with 
the exception of boating, were tried and 
found to be suitable after obvious al¬ 
lowances had been made for greater 
counsellor assistance, less haste, infinite 
patience and understanding of indivi¬ 
dual handicaps. Nature hikes, over¬ 
nights, crafts, games, play-acting, In¬ 
dian night, excursions, these and many 


146 


Canadian Camping 




other regular activities are suitable 
when modified as to simplicity of de¬ 
mand upon the camper and lower¬ 
geared timing. Time tables had to be 
modified several times to allow for 
longer rest periods and more time for 
campers to wash and dress and to get 
from one place to another because 
movement and muscular co-ordination 
is much slower than with normal 
children. 

We found that counsellors who had 
good recommendations from other 
camps made good leaders with the 
seriously retarded campers. Perhaps 
this is, in part, because handicapped 
children have the same basic human 
needs as all people. These are such 
needs as to be liked by others and to 
learn to like others, to achieve and to 
be helped to achieve, and to be limited 
to socially desirable learnings and be¬ 
haviour. However, throughout our en¬ 
tire programme from the counsellors’ 
training course, to the last farewell, the 
staff was aware that in addition to 
these common human needs, which any 
good camp tries to meet, our children 
had special concerns. For example, our 
children have special needs to learn to 
obey signals, since few, if any of them 
can read or have the benefit of social 
learnings that come from varied social 
experiences. It was discovered after 
much trial and error that teaching 
them to crouch at the blow of a whistle 
was the best way to get their attention 
in response to this particular signal. 
Various levels of social and physical 
development meant various levels of 
participation in activities. For example, 
whereas some children could actually 
lead a sing-song of the whole camp, 
others could barely participate. For 
some who may have been protected 
from or excluded from their neighbour-

Moccasins are the shoes of the bush 
and the canoe, the shoes of the forest 
children. 

Those who wear moccasins go about 
quietly, disturbing little, allowing the 
wearer to see and to hear all about him, 
unafraid. 

Those who come to wear the Magic 
Moccasins, get to know the secret 
places, hear the unfamiliar sounds, the 
feel of new things, the smell and taste 
of the unusual. 

The Magic Moccasins take you to all 
the varied loveliness of living things 
which God has created in this, your 
homeland. 

Once you wear the Magic Moccasins, 
you will find 

— the saskatoons, sweet berries of the 
summer time. 

— the biggest blueberries 

— the sun-warmed flavour of ripe 
raspberries 

— the bitter, puckering taste of 
choke-cherries 

— the cool savour of basswood bark 

The Magic Moccasins will carry you 
along through lakes and streams, lined 
with the many shades of the green of 
trees; decorated along the edges with 
flaming cardinal flowers,* iris, and pur¬ 
ple joepie weed; covered with yellow 
and white water lilies. 

The Magic Moccasins will carry you 
to the highest places, where you can 
look to the far horizon; to the very 
edge of the dome of the cloudless sky; 
where you can look down into the 


From Camp Mazinaw, Mr. G. R. 
Blackstock has sent us the story of the 
Wearers of the Magic Moccasins, an 
Indian legend whose charm and philo¬ 
sophy are transposed to our own way of 
living, in a way campers can easily 
grasp. 


echoing valleys and into the shadowless 
blue of deep water. 

The Wearers will come to know the 
busy ways of the beaver, the slow, un¬ 
caring way of the porky, the stately way 
of the skunk, the inquisitive, noisy man¬ 
ners of the racoon, the scurrying, chat¬ 
tering way of the squirrels and 
chipmunks. Like Hiawatha, you will 
come to call all manner of living crea¬ 
tures, Brother! 

If you put on these Magic Moccasins, 
you will find the cool valleys, where the 
light-footed deer stand among small 
birches and massive basswoods; and the 
hot, bare hillsides, where the ant-tun- 
nelled stumps linger, showing the marks 
of the hungry bear. 

Here at camp, we would want you 
to become the Wearers of the Magic 
Moccasins, so that you can romp joy¬ 
ously through the days, aware of all the 
living world about you, even as Jesus 
did, long ago, pausing to marvel at the 
beauty and the wonder and the loveli¬ 
ness of it all. 

Be ye Wearers of the Magic Mocca¬ 
sins in the bushland of your homeland 
in these, the Moons of summertime!

hood play group, the special need was 
to learn how to have fun with others, 
sharing, taking turns, being part of a 
team. And of course, the special need 
to be taught with great patience 
through repetition, routine and imita¬ 
tion, meant going over the same activity 
endless times. Would this be boring for 
the counsellors? No. The great rewards 
to the counsellors in seeing the child 
progress are so personally satisfying, 
that it was common for an experienced 
counsellor to say that this kind of camp 
meant more to them than any previous 
experience. It is interesting that all 
counsellors except one, want to return 
again this year. 

Although the final analyses of re¬ 
search records is not completed, we 
have some tentative conclusions which 
are most encouraging. Individual record 


charts filled out daily by the counsellors 
for each of his campers, prove that 
these children readily adjusted to a 
camping situation. They learned new 
skills, their behaviour improved and 
they developed social relationships with 
other campers. 

Follow-up reports from teachers in 
the special O.A.R.G. Schools and from 
parents, indicate that a large number 
of parents and teachers noticed definite 
improvements in the campers’ sociabili¬ 
ty and friendliness upon their return 
from camp. A typical remark from a 
parent is, that: “Bobby now plays 
better with neighbourhood children” or 
“He still wants to do the things he 
learned at camp” or “He had the best 
time of his life”.

fortunate children who could attend Bel- 
wood last summer, had the time of their

lives. Unfortunately, because we were 
soon filled up, many applicants could not 
be served last year. But this is just the 
beginning of camps for retarded child¬ 
ren. We are beginning to learn what 
should go into the ideal camp site for 
these children. Their camp will need 
special facilities, because these are 
special children. Ideally, each cabin 
would have six campers (all sleeping 
on lower bunks) and quarters for two 
counsellors. Washroom and toilet facili¬ 
ties should be in or adjoining the cabin. 
The whole camp area should be fenced 
in, to protect possible wanderers. It 
should be as safe as a bank, with all 
possible booby-traps both natural and 
man-made eliminated. It should be as 
beautiful as the Great Canadian out¬ 
doors can be, with wooded areas, ooen 
spaces and safe, shallow, sandy beaches. 
It should have a swimming pool, be¬ 
cause warm, shallow water is very im¬ 
portant for their swimming. 

Ten years ago, there was virtually 
not a day school nor a recreation 
programme nor even an organization 
advancing the cause of providing com¬ 
munity services for the intellectually 
least gifted in our whole country. To¬ 
day, in every province of Canada, 
special local schools exist, and in each 
province, there is an association for the 
help of retarded children. Tomorrow, 
there will be recreation programmes, 
sheltered workshops, diagnostic clinics 
and many other needed services, includ¬ 
ing soecial summer camps. Perhaps 
these camps will be built and based on 
the information gathered at Belwood.

Gradually, talk became centered on the 
rappel, the highlight of “Rock School”. 

Rappeling is the climber’s method of 
descending a steep pitch by means of 
a rope doubled round a projection. 
When a young boy thinks of mountain 
climbing, a picture of a climber em¬ 
ploying a free rappel is very often the 
first thing that comes to mind. For this 
reason, rappel instruction was included 
in “Rock School” programme as an 
“extra-curricular activity”, even though 
the nature of our climbs would not 
necessitate the use of this technique. 

“Rock School” was just the begin¬ 
ning of this new experience. Real 
mountain climbing was yet in the 
offing. With their counsellors, the boys 
eagerly discussed which mountain they 
would assault, what route they would 
take, and where they would establish 
their base camp. 


The mountains in the vicinity of 
Hector are about seven thousand feet 
high (1,500 feet above Gamp). Reach¬ 
ing one of these summits would be a 
short scramble for a mountaineer, but 
it is an impressive accomplishment for 
a fifteen year-old lad. During the course 
of the summer, assaults were made on 
five different peaks, two of which were 
scaled to the summit. A highlight of 
the programme was what is believed 
to have been a “first assault” on Mount 
Faulkner, and the ceremony by which 
it was named in honor of a former 
director of the camp. 

Our experiment in mountain climb¬ 
ing has shown us that adventure is 
provided, and development of the spirit, 
mind, and body, naturally follow, when 
a boy is methodically introduced to the 4 
wonderful world of mountains.

It was with this thought in mind that the new ACA song book 
was developed. Thousands of camping people responded to ques¬ 
tionnaires which the compiling committee used in developing the 
new book. 


The book is functional and practical. Between its covers are 
the old favourites of camping groups plus new songs which it is 

anticipated, will soon become fav¬ 
ourites. The inexperienced coun¬ 
selor can find songs which are 
easily sung. There is an excellent 
selection of an inspiring variety 
of the best beloved songs for tra¬ 
ditional occasions and the most 
meaningful for special occasions. 

Response has been most en¬ 
thusiastic. Copies can be obtained 
from the American Camping 
Association, Martinsville, Indiana. 
Prices: 1 to 24 copies, 35 c each; 
25-49 copies, 30c each; 50 or 
more copies, 25c each.

that they are off the beaten path. Under 
the delusion that nobody knows them 
and nobody cares, they scatter refuse, 
they yell, they are profane, they roar 
out ribald songs. Gould we conceivably 
be conditioning our campers for that 
sort of adulthood? 

What can we do? In our own camps 
we can set high standards and provide 
campers with acceptable techniques for 
outdoor living. We can strive to create 
a feeling of respect for the outdoors and 
for the property and rights of others. 
We can work to develop a missionary 
spirit which will stay with campers all 
their lives, and make them want to 
teach others the things they have 
learned. 

We COULD start a campaign to 
clean up and cure these ugly sores 
civilization has wrought in camping 
territory and make them again, beauti¬ 
ful campsites.
